beats.text: England, seventeen ninety-six. A doctor takes pus from a milkmaid's hand. And scratches it into the arm of an eight-year-old boy.
Weeks later, he infects the same boy with smallpox. On purpose.
Smallpox killed about three in ten people who caught it. Many survivors were scarred, or blind.
The doctor was Edward Jenner. He had heard that milkmaids who caught cowpox, a mild disease from cows, never got smallpox.
But would it work? The boy, James Phipps, never got sick.
So the cowpox trick spread. People were scared. A famous cartoon showed vaccinated people growing cows. But the name stuck: vaccination, from vacca, Latin for cow.
Then the world vaccinated, country by country, for almost two hundred years.
In nineteen eighty, smallpox was declared gone. The only human disease ever eradicated.
It all started with one boy, one milkmaid, and a cow named Blossom.

sources: May 1796: Edward Jenner inoculated 8-year-old James Phipps with matter from a cowpox sore of milkmaid Sarah Nelmes; July 1796 he exposed him to smallpox; Phipps stayed healthy. WHO, 'History of smallpox vaccination'.

Smallpox killed about 3 in 10 people infected (NIAID via Live Science); vaccination from Latin vacca = cow (Pfizer, 'Smallpox vanquished'); declared eradicated in 1980, the only human disease eradicated so far (WHO; Our World in Data).

Cowpox from Sarah Nelmes, who caught it from a cow called Blossom (Jenner Institute / Dr Jenner's House; Blossom's hide hangs in St George's Medical School library). James Gillray, 'The Cow-Pock – or – the Wonderful Effects of the New Inoculation!' (1802), public domain. Many smallpox survivors were scarred, some blinded (WHO/CDC).
